name: Temple of Poseidon
blurb: Doric marble temple on a sea cliff, 5th century BC · Lord Byron carved his own name into one of its marble columns in 1810 — the graffiti is still legible today
source: Wikimedia Commons: Temple of Poseidon perspective at Cape Sounion Greece.jpg

name: Tulum
blurb: Maya walled port perched on cliffs above the Caribbean, 13th century · Its original name meant 'dawn' — the cliffs face due east, where the Maya watched the sun rise over the sea
source: Wikimedia Commons: Tulum - God of the Winds Temple 03.JPG

name: Venus of Willendorf
blurb: c. 28,000–25,000 BC · Natural History Museum, Vienna — carved before farming, writing, or the wheel existed, making her one of the oldest known artworks by tens of thousands of years
source: Wikimedia Commons: Venus von Willendorf 01.jpg

name: Vitruvian Man
blurb: Leonardo da Vinci's study of human proportions (c. 1490) · Kept in storage almost permanently, light-sensitive on paper — shown publicly only a few weeks every six years
source: Wikimedia Commons: Da Vinci Vitruve Luc Viatour.jpg

name: Windsor Castle
blurb: The world's oldest inhabited castle, a royal residence west of London since 1070 · A 1992 fire tore through 100-plus rooms — restoration was paid for by opening Buckingham Palace to visitors
source: Wikimedia Commons: Castle View from Alexandra Park - Round Tower, St George’s Chapel and the Curfew Tower. Windsor, UK.jpg

name: Winged Victory of Samothrace
blurb: c. 200–190 BC · Discovered shattered on a Greek island in 1863 — a missing hand turned up decades later, never reattached
source: Wikimedia Commons: Nike of Samothrake Louvre Ma2369 n4.jpg

name: Winter Palace
blurb: Baroque imperial palace, completed 1762 · The 1917 'storming' was almost bloodless — the dramatic version is a staged 1920 re-enactment
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Winter Palace and the Alexander Column, Saint Petersburg, Russia.jpg

name: Wright Flyer
blurb: The machine of the first powered flight, Kitty Hawk 1903 · Its first powered flight covered about 120 feet in 12 seconds — shorter than the wingspan of a Boeing 747
source: Wikimedia Commons: First flight3.jpg

name: Alfred Jewel
blurb: Anglo-Saxon gold and enamel aestel inscribed for King Alfred, 9th century AD · Found by a farmer ploughing in 1693, near where Alfred hid from Vikings — inscribed 'Alfred ordered me made'
source: Wikimedia Commons: Alfred Jewel Ashmolean 2014.JPG

name: Amber Fort
blurb: Rajput hilltop fort-palace of pale sandstone above Jaipur, 16th–17th century · Its Sheesh Mahal, 'Mirror Palace,' is lined with mirrors — one candle makes it glitter like starlight
source: Wikimedia Commons: Amber Fort, Jaipur, 20191219 1045 9589.jpg

name: Arc de Triomphe
blurb: Napoleonic triumphal arch, completed 1836 · Beneath it burns an eternal flame, relit by hand nightly since 1923, even under Nazi occupation
source: Wikimedia Commons: Arc Triomphe.jpg

name: Arena of Verona
blurb: Roman amphitheatre still used for opera, 1st century AD · Only four arches of its outer wall survive, most fell in a 12th-century quake — it's hosted opera since 1913
source: Wikimedia Commons: Verona Arena 01.jpg

name: Bagan
blurb: Myanmar's plain studded with thousands of Buddhist temples, 11th–13th century · A hasty 1990s restoration, criticised for inauthentic materials, delayed its UNESCO recognition until 2019
source: Wikimedia Commons: Old Bagan, Myanmar, Landscape of ancient Bagan city.jpg

name: Bayon Temple
blurb: Temple of smiling stone faces (late 12th century) · Carved with roughly 200 giant smiling faces, thought to merge its king with a compassionate Buddhist deity
source: Wikimedia Commons: Angkor - Bayon - 004 Tower Faces (8581824754).jpg

name: The Blue Mosque
blurb: Ottoman imperial mosque with six minarets (1616) · Its six minarets matched Mecca's holiest mosque, a scandal — the sultan paid for a seventh minaret there
source: Wikimedia Commons: Exterior of Sultan Ahmed I Mosque in Istanbul, Turkey 002.jpg

name: Book of Kells
blurb: Illuminated Gospel manuscript (c. 800 AD) · Hidden in its decoration is a tiny doodle of a cat chasing a mouse — monks slipped in playful marginalia
source: Wikimedia Commons: KellsFol034rChiRhoMonogram.jpg

name: Borobudur
blurb: World's largest Buddhist temple (9th century) · Abandoned and buried under ash and jungle, it was rediscovered in 1814 on Raffles's orders
source: Wikimedia Commons: Borobudur-Temple-Park Indonesia Stupas-of-Borobudur-04.jpg

name: Boudhanath
blurb: One of the world's largest Buddhist stupas, its painted all-seeing eyes watching over Kathmandu
source: Wikimedia Commons: Boudhanath stupa, Kathmandu 01.jpg

name: Buckingham Palace
blurb: London residence of the British monarch, remodelled 1913 · In 1982, an intruder scaled the wall and sat on the Queen's bed chatting with her, unnoticed
source: Wikimedia Commons: Buckingham Palace east front facade.jpg

name: Catalan Atlas
blurb: Illuminated medieval world map showing Mansa Musa of Mali enthroned, holding a gold nugget to signal he was the richest man alive, 1375 · Bibliothèque nationale de France
source: Wikimedia Commons: 1375 Atlas Catalan, Europe 02.jpg
mcq: Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry

name: Catherine Palace
blurb: Rococo imperial palace, rebuilt 1752-56 · Its famed Amber Room vanished in Nazi looting, never found — today's version is a 2003 replica
source: Wikimedia Commons: 00 5105 Catherine Palace (Большой Екатерининский дворец) in Pushkin, Russia.jpg

name: Château de Chambord
blurb: France's most flamboyant Loire château, its famous double-helix staircase rumoured to have been sketched by Leonardo da Vinci, begun for François I in 1519
source: Wikimedia Commons: France Loir-et-Cher Chambord Chateau 01.jpg
image_author: No machine-readable author provided. Calips assumed (based on copyright claims).

name: Charioteer of Delphi
blurb: Serene bronze victor cast for Delphi's sanctuary, 478 BC · It survived only because a rockslide buried it soon after — most ancient bronzes were melted down
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Charioteer of Delphi, 478 BC, AM of Delphi, 201441.jpg

name: Cologne Cathedral
blurb: Germany's soaring Gothic cathedral of twin openwork spires, completed in 1880 · Construction stalled 300 years — a medieval crane sat atop the tower so long it became a landmark itself
source: Wikimedia Commons: Cologne Germany Cologne-Cathedral-West-Facade-01.jpg

name: Ctesiphon
blurb: The soaring brick arch of a Persian palace near Baghdad, 6th century AD · Its brick vault is still the largest unreinforced arch on Earth, built with no supporting frame
source: Wikimedia Commons: 001125-TaqKasra-Iraq-IMG 7914-2.jpg

name: Delphi Temple
blurb: Sanctuary of the Delphic oracle, 4th century BC · Geologists think the oracle's trance came from gases seeping through a fault beneath the temple floor
source: Wikimedia Commons: Delphes, Grèce. Temple d'Apollon. Six colonnes.jpg

name: Edinburgh Castle
blurb: Scotland's royal fortress atop a volcanic crag — besieged more than any other place in Britain, roughly 26 times across 1,100 years
source: Wikimedia Commons: Edinburgh Castle Rock.jpg

name: Fasil Ghebbi
blurb: Ethiopia's stone castle-citadel at Gondar, nicknamed 'the Camelot of Africa', 17th century. · Built with Portuguese, Indian and Jesuit craftsmen, giving it battlements startlingly European
source: Wikimedia Commons: Fasil Ghebbi (6821475763).jpg

name: The Forbidden City
blurb: Chinese imperial palace (1420) · Folklore claims 9,999.5 rooms, one short of Heaven's mythical 10,000 — a modern survey counted around 8,700
source: Wikimedia Commons: Beijing China Forbidden-City-03.jpg

name: Great Buddha of Kamakura
blurb: Bronze Amida Buddha (1252) · It once sat inside a temple hall — repeated tsunamis washed the hall away, so for centuries it's sat outdoors
source: Wikimedia Commons: Kamakura Budda Daibutsu front 1885.jpg

name: Great Enclosure Zimbabwe
blurb: Massive dry-stone walled royal enclosure, 11th–15th century AD · Colonial officials insisted outsiders built it — archaeology confirmed it was the Shona's ancestors' work
source: Wikimedia Commons: East Wall Great Enclosure (47614139601).jpg
image_author: Andrew Moore from Johannesburg, South Africa

name: Great Mosque of Djenné
blurb: The world's largest mud-brick building, in Mali, rebuilt in 1907 · Every year the whole town turns out to re-plaster its mud walls by hand — rain washes some away annually
source: Wikimedia Commons: Great Mosque of Djenné 1.jpg

name: Gundestrup Cauldron
blurb: Ornate Iron Age silver vessel with Celtic mythological reliefs, c. 150–1 BC · Found dismantled in a Danish peat bog, styled from far-off origins — likely a ritual offering
source: Wikimedia Commons: Gundestrup cauldron - F.I.4277.jpg

name: Hadrian's Villa
blurb: Emperor Hadrian's retreat with the arched Canopus pool, 2nd century AD · Hadrian filled it with replicas from his travels, plus a canal honouring Antinous, who drowned in the Nile
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Canopus, Hadrian's Villa, Tivoli (14759103250).jpg

name: Code of Hammurabi
blurb: c. 1754 BC · Louvre, Paris — one of the oldest deciphered law codes of real length, and the source of the phrase 'an eye for an eye'
source: Wikimedia Commons: P1050763 Louvre code Hammurabi face rwk.JPG

name: Himeji Castle
blurb: Japan's grandest samurai-era castle (1609) · Nicknamed the White Heron Castle, it survived WWII bombing — one bomb hit it but never exploded
source: Wikimedia Commons: Himeji Castle 0804 1.jpg

name: Imperial State Crown
blurb: 1937 · Tower of London, London — set with over 2,800 diamonds, it's worn by the monarch only a few times a year, most famously at the State Opening of Parliament
source: Wikimedia Commons: ImperialStateCrown.jpg

name: Karnak
blurb: Egypt's vast temple of Amun and its forest of columns, at Luxor · Built by 30-plus pharaohs over 2,000 years — its Great Hypostyle Hall alone packs 134 giant columns
source: Wikimedia Commons: Karnak Temple Great Hypostyle Hall 2014.jpg

name: Lascaux Cave Paintings
blurb: c. 17,000 BC · The real cave has been sealed since 1963 — tourists' breath grew mould on it; today's visit is a replica
source: Wikimedia Commons: Lascaux painting.jpg

name: Leshan Giant Buddha
blurb: The world’s tallest pre-modern stone Buddha, carved into a river cliff, 713–803 AD · A monk carved it hoping the Buddha would calm a river confluence that kept sinking boats
source: Wikimedia Commons: Leshan Giant Buddha, March 2000 04.jpg

name: Lewis Chessmen
blurb: c. 1150–1200 AD · British Museum, London — their bug-eyed, beard-chewing berserker rooks helped inspire the wizard's chess set in the Harry Potter films
source: Wikimedia Commons: NMSLewisChessmen28.jpg

name: Lindisfarne Gospels
blurb: Illuminated Latin gospel book with carpet pages, c. AD 700 · Made on Lindisfarne decades before the 793 Viking raid that marks the Viking Age's start
source: Wikimedia Commons: Meister des Book of Lindisfarne 002.jpg
mcq: Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry

name: Magna Carta
blurb: 1215 AD · Pope Innocent III annulled it within ten weeks — its legend only took hold centuries later
source: Wikimedia Commons: Magna Carta (British Library Cotton MS Augustus II.106).jpg
image_author: Original authors were the barons and King John of England. Uploaded by Earthsound.

name: Meteora
blurb: Greek Orthodox monasteries perched atop sheer rock pinnacles — one doubled as a villain's lair in the Bond film For Your Eyes Only
source: Wikimedia Commons: Meteora, 09.jpg

name: Mildenhall Treasure
blurb: Roman silver hoard with the Oceanus Great Dish, 4th century AD · Ploughed up by a Suffolk farmer in 1942 — owners kept it quiet before its Roman origins were sorted out
source: Wikimedia Commons: Mildenhall Great Dish, Late Roman period, silver - British Museum - DSC01383.jpg

name: Mycenae Lion Gate
blurb: Monumental citadel gateway relief, c. 1250 BC · Homer called Mycenae 'rich in gold' — confirmed when excavators found gold death masks inside this gate
source: Wikimedia Commons: Lions Gate detail.JPG

name: Naqsh-e Rustam
blurb: Cliff carved with the cross-shaped tombs of Persia's Achaemenid kings · A Persian king later added a relief of a Roman emperor kneeling in submission, Rome's worst defeat
source: Wikimedia Commons: Tombs of Achaemenid Kings at Naqsh-e Rustam (4885711726).jpg
image_author: A.Davey from Portland, Oregon, EE UU

name: Nazca Lines
blurb: Giant desert geoglyphs (500 BC – 500 AD) · Carved so large they're unrecognisable from the ground, unnoticed until airplanes flew overhead in the 1920s
source: Wikimedia Commons: Líneas de Nazca, Nazca, Perú, 2015-07-29, DD 52.JPG

name: Nebra Sky Disc
blurb: Bronze Age astronomical disc with gold sun, moon and stars, c. 1600 BC · Illegally dug up by looters in 1999, recovered two years later in a police sting on the black market
source: Wikimedia Commons: Himmelsscheibe von Nebra - Landesmuseum für Vorgeschichte in Halle - HD.jpg

name: Olmec Colossal Head
blurb: Giant basalt head of an Olmec ruler (1200–400 BC) · Each head is thought a real ruler's portrait in a ballgame helmet — hauled miles without wheels
source: Wikimedia Commons: Olmec Colossal Head, San Lorenzo, Veracruz, 1200-600 BC.jpg

name: Oseberg Ship
blurb: A Viking queen's burial ship, interred c. 834, unearthed 1904 · Grave robbers found the mound first but missed most treasures — blue clay preserved the wood
source: Wikimedia Commons: Oseberg Ship - Viking Ship Museum (Oslo).jpg

name: Palace of Versailles
blurb: Royal palace expanded under Louis XIV, 17th century · France smuggled Venetian glassmakers out of Italy, breaking a monopoly, to make its Hall of Mirrors
source: Wikimedia Commons: Garden facade of the Palace of Versailles 2.jpg

name: Pantheon Rome
blurb: Former Roman temple, rebuilt c. AD 113–125 · Its dome has an open hole at the top — rain falls through onto a marble floor built with drains
source: Wikimedia Commons: Pantheon Rom 1 cropped.jpg

name: Persepolis
blurb: Gateway of the Achaemenid kings' ceremonial capital · Alexander's army burned it down in 330 BC — payback for Athens, or a drunken party, sources disagree
source: Wikimedia Commons: Persepolis – Gate of All Nations 02.jpg

name: Phaistos Disc
blurb: Crete's undeciphered stamped-clay riddle, c. 1700 BC · No one has found a second example of its stamped symbols — some wonder, half-jokingly, if it's a hoax
source: Wikimedia Commons: Phaistos Disc — Side A.jpg

name: Piri Reis Map
blurb: Ottoman gazelle-skin map of the Atlantic coasts that explicitly cites a now-lost map by Christopher Columbus as one of its sources, 1513 · Topkapi Palace Museum, Istanbul
source: Wikimedia Commons: Piri reis world map 01.jpg

name: Pompeii Forum
blurb: Civic square of the buried Roman city, destroyed AD 79 · The eerily lifelike victim casts weren't bodies — plaster poured into voids left in the hardened ash
source: Wikimedia Commons: Forum in Pompeii 2.jpg

name: Ponte Vecchio
blurb: Medieval stone bridge lined with shops, rebuilt 1345 · Retreating Nazis destroyed every other Florence bridge in 1944 — this one survived on Hitler's own orders
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ponte Vecchio sobre el río Arno, Florencia, Italia, 2022-09-19, DD 02.jpg

name: Portland Vase
blurb: Roman cameo-glass vase with white figures on cobalt blue, 1st century AD · Smashed into some 200 pieces by a drunk visitor at the British Museum in 1845, pieced back together since
source: Wikimedia Commons: Portland Vase BM Gem4036 n1 resized white-balanced white bg.png

name: Potala Palace
blurb: Former palace of the Dalai Lamas (1649) · Standing above 3,700 metres, among the highest palaces ever built — workers hauled materials up by hand
source: Wikimedia Commons: Potala Palace, former residence of Dalai Lama, 2006.jpg

name: Registan
blurb: Samarkand's grand plaza framed by three Timurid madrasas, 15th–17th century · One madrasa breaks Islamic tradition — its facade shows tigers chasing deer, faces peeking from suns
source: Wikimedia Commons: Registan square, Samarkand, Uzbekistan.jpg

name: Rila Monastery
blurb: Bulgaria's grandest Orthodox monastery, its striped arcades ringed by mountains · Through nearly five centuries of Ottoman rule, the monastery kept Bulgarian language and learning alive
source: Wikimedia Commons: 2016-07-31 Bulgaria, Rila Monastery DSC 9213 DxO.jpg

name: Roman Forum
blurb: Temple of Saturn, rebuilt 4th century AD after a fire (first dedicated 497 BC) · For centuries after Rome fell it was a cow pasture, nicknamed 'Campo Vaccino,' before excavators dug it out
source: Wikimedia Commons: Roman Forum Temple of Saturn.jpg

name: Rosetta Stone
blurb: 196 BC · The same decree carved three times, in hieroglyphs, Demotic, and Greek — which is what let Champollion crack hieroglyphs at last
source: Wikimedia Commons: Rosetta Stone - front face - corrected image.jpg

name: Sacré-Cœur
blurb: The white-domed basilica crowning Montmartre above Paris, completed in 1914 · Built as an act of penance after France's 1870-71 defeat and the bloody suppression of the Paris Commune
source: Wikimedia Commons: Basilique du Sacré-Cœur de Montmartre - Paris - GT-01 - 2024.jpg

name: Sacsayhuamán
blurb: Inca citadel of vast interlocking stones above Cusco, 15th century · Stones weighing over 100 tonnes fit so tight a knife can't slide between — how the Inca moved them is unclear
source: Wikimedia Commons: Sacsayhuamán, Cusco, Perú, 2015-07-31, DD 05.JPG

name: Schoenbrunn Palace
blurb: Habsburg summer palace, largely rebuilt 1740s-1750s · Six-year-old Mozart did perform here in 1762 — his proposal to young Marie Antoinette is unconfirmed legend
source: Wikimedia Commons: Wien - Schloss Schönbrunn.JPG
mcq: Monastery and Site of the Escorial

name: The School of Athens
blurb: Raphael, 1509–1511 · Raphael gave the philosophers contemporaries' faces — Plato resembles Leonardo, Heraclitus, Michelangelo
source: Wikimedia Commons: "The School of Athens" by Raffaello Sanzio da Urbino.jpg

name: Segovia Aqueduct
blurb: Roman Spain's towering double-tier aqueduct of dry-laid granite, c. 100 AD · Legend says the Devil built it overnight for a girl's soul — Romans actually built it without mortar
source: Wikimedia Commons: Acueducto de Segovia 01.jpg

name: St Peter's Basilica
blurb: Renaissance basilica, completed 1626 · Funding for it, raised partly by selling indulgences, helped push Luther to launch the Reformation
source: Wikimedia Commons: Facade of Saint Peter's Basilica.jpg

name: St Stephen's Cathedral
blurb: Vienna's Gothic cathedral with its dazzling patterned tiled roof · Its patterned roof uses 230,000-plus glazed tiles, forming a mosaic of the double-headed Habsburg eagle
source: Wikimedia Commons: Wien - Stephansdom (1).JPG

name: Staffordshire Hoard
blurb: Largest hoard of Anglo-Saxon gold and silver metalwork, 7th century AD · Found in 2009 by an amateur with a metal detector in a Staffordshire field — almost all war-gear
source: Wikimedia Commons: Sheet Gold Plaque, Staffordshire Hoard.jpg
image_author: Jon Callas from San Jose, USA

name: Temple of Hatshepsut
blurb: Terraced mortuary temple of a female pharaoh at Deir el-Bahari, 15th century BC · After her death, her images were hacked out and her name chiselled off, erasing a woman who ruled as pharaoh
source: Wikimedia Commons: Temple of Hatshepsut, Deir el-Bahari, Luxor, Egypt.jpg

name: Temple of Heaven
blurb: Imperial altar of prayer for good harvests (1420) · Its main hall was built without a single nail — held together purely by interlocking joints and brackets
source: Wikimedia Commons: 20200110 Temple of Heaven-1.jpg
mcq: Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry

name: Tikal
blurb: Maya temple-pyramid towering over the Guatemalan rainforest, c. 700 AD — its jungle-topped silhouette played the rebel base on Yavin 4 in the original Star Wars
source: Wikimedia Commons: Temple of the Great Jaguar, Tikal, Petén, Guatemala.jpg

name: Tower of London
blurb: Royal castle founded 1066–1078 · Legend holds the kingdom falls if its ravens leave — wings clipped for centuries, just in case
source: Wikimedia Commons: London, Tower of London -- 2016 -- 4791.jpg

name: Uffington White Horse
blurb: Britain's stylised chalk hill-figure above Oxfordshire, cut c. 1000 BC — legend places St George's dragon-slaying on the bare hill just below it
source: Wikimedia Commons: Aerial View of Uffington White Horse at Harvest Time - geograph.org.uk - 4403449.jpg

name: Wat Arun
blurb: Bangkok's Temple of Dawn and its porcelain-clad spire on the Chao Phraya · Its glittering surface is broken Chinese porcelain, repurposed from ships' ballast unloaded in Bangkok's port
source: Wikimedia Commons: WAT ARUN TEMPLE CHAO PRAYA RIVER BANGKOK THAILAND FEB 2012 (6985905427).jpg

name: Westminster Abbey
variants: collegiate church of st peter westminster
blurb: Gothic royal church, mainly 13th–16th century · Every English coronation since 1066 has happened here, on a chair that once held the Stone of Scone
source: Wikimedia Commons: Westminster Abbey (St. Peter) (47537372181).jpg

name: Court of the Lions
blurb: Fountain courtyard of the Alhambra (14th century) · Granada, Spain — its twelve marble lions are one of the rare figurative sculptures in Islamic art, which traditionally avoided depicting animals and people
source: Wikimedia Commons: Fountain patio de los Leones Alhambra Granada Spain.jpg

name: The Arnolfini Portrait
blurb: Jan van Eyck, 1434 · National Gallery, London — look for the tiny convex mirror on the back wall: it reflects the whole room, including two figures who may be the painter himself
source: Wikimedia Commons: Van Eyck - Arnolfini Portrait.jpg

name: Aksum
blurb: Towering carved granite stelae of an ancient Ethiopian kingdom, c. 4th century AD — one was looted by Mussolini's Italy in 1937 and only returned, in pieces, by cargo plane in 2005
source: Wikimedia Commons: Stela in Main Stelae Field - Axum (Aksum) - Ethiopia - 01 (8701108913).jpg
image_author: Adam Jones from Kelowna, BC, Canada

name: Baalbek
blurb: Lebanon's colossal Roman temple complex, 2nd century AD — raised on some of the largest cut stones ever used in construction, including a nearby block weighing close to 1,000 tonnes
source: Wikimedia Commons: Lebanon, Baalbek, Temple of Bacchus.jpg

name: Baths of Caracalla
blurb: Monumental public bathing complex, completed AD 216 · Its ruins inspired the grand vaulted halls of New York's original Penn Station and Chicago's Union Station
source: Wikimedia Commons: Baths of Caracalla 2.JPG

name: Belém Tower
blurb: Manueline fortress-tower guarding Lisbon's harbour, early 16th century · One carved gargoyle is a rhinoceros, based on a famous woodcut whose artist never actually saw one
source: Wikimedia Commons: Torre Belém April 2009-4a.jpg

name: Benin Bronzes
blurb: Brass palace plaques of the Kingdom of Benin, 15th–16th century · Despite the name, most are brass, cast by lost-wax technique — British forces looted the palace in 1897
source: Wikimedia Commons: At the British Museum 2024 017.jpg

name: Carnac Stones
blurb: Brittany’s miles-long rows of standing stones — the largest gathering of megaliths on Earth, c. 3300 BC
source: Wikimedia Commons: Carnac Standing Stones Alignment, Carnac, Brittany - panoramio.jpg

name: Chan Chan
blurb: The vast adobe capital of the Chimú kingdom on Peru's coast, c. 1400 · The largest adobe city ever built in the Americas — also among the most endangered, in El Niño rains
source: Wikimedia Commons: Vast Abobe Ruins at Chan Chan.JPG

name: Chartres Cathedral
variants: cathedral of our lady of chartres
blurb: Rebuilt after the 1194 fire with its stained glass intact, mainly 12th–13th century · Its cobalt 'Chartres blue' stained glass uses a medieval recipe never fully reproduced since
source: Wikimedia Commons: Cathedral Notre Dame, Chartres (3729893669).jpg
image_author: Elliott Brown from Birmingham, United Kingdom

name: Codex Sinaiticus
blurb: One of the oldest Bibles in Greek, with a complete New Testament, 4th century AD · Its pages are split across four institutions — the Sinai monastery where found disputes how they got there
source: Wikimedia Commons: Codex Sinaiticus Matthew 1,1-2,5.JPG

name: Column of Marcus Aurelius
blurb: Rome's spiralling marble war record — deliberately modelled on Trajan's Column, but starring a very different, much bloodier war, 2nd century AD
source: Wikimedia Commons: Column of Marcus Aurelius, Rome.jpg

name: Copán
blurb: Maya city in Honduras renowned for its intricately carved stone stelae, c. 700 AD · Its Hieroglyphic Stairway carries the longest known Maya inscription — reassembled wrong, order still debated
source: Wikimedia Commons: Copán Maya stelae 2.jpg

name: Cyrus Cylinder
blurb: Clay cylinder in which Cyrus the Great, fresh off conquering Babylon in 539 BC, freed its captives and restored their gods — later hailed as history's first human-rights charter
source: Wikimedia Commons: Cyrus Cylinder 2.jpg

name: Dead Sea Scrolls
blurb: Discovered in 1947 when a Bedouin shepherd boy threw a rock into a cave and heard something break
attribution: Photography by Ardon Bar Hama (see [2], author of original document is unknown.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Great Isaiah Scroll Ch53.jpg
image_author: Photography by Ardon Bar Hama (see [2], author of original document is unknown.

name: Diamond Sutra
blurb: Woodblock-printed Buddhist scroll dated 868 AD — the world's earliest complete dated printed book, nearly 600 years before Gutenberg · British Library, London
source: Wikimedia Commons: Diamond Sutra of 868 AD - The Diamond Sutra (868), frontispiece and text - BL Or. 8210-P.2.jpg
image_author: This file has been provided by the British Library from its digital collections. Links to the British Library's website may be broken as the library recovers from a October 2023 cyber attack, and will be updated once material becomes accessible online. For more information on the attack see: https://www.bl.uk/about/cyber-attack

name: Elgin Marbles
blurb: c. 447–438 BC · British Museum, London — at the center of a 200-year tug-of-war between Athens and London over whether they belong on the Parthenon
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Parthenon Frieze - British Museum - Joy of Museums.jpg

name: Ghent Altarpiece
blurb: Begun by Hubert van Eyck, completed by his brother Jan in 1432 — the most stolen artwork in history · Ghent, Belgium
attribution: Jan van Eyck (presumably Hubert van Eyck)
source: Wikimedia Commons: Lamgods open.jpg
image_author: Jan van Eyck / Presumably Hubert van Eyck

name: Gutenberg Bible
blurb: First major book printed in Europe with movable type (1455) · About 49 copies survive worldwide
attribution: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress
source: Wikimedia Commons: Gutenberg Bible B42 Genesis.JPG
image_author: Original by Johannes Gutenberg (printer), Scan by Jossi

name: Gyeongbokgung
blurb: Seoul's grand royal palace of the Joseon dynasty, first built in 1395 · Left in ruins two centuries after invasion, rebuilt in 1867 — Japan then built its HQ right in front
source: Wikimedia Commons: Front view of the Imperial Throne Hall Geunjeongjeon at Gyeongbokgung Palace with blue sky in Seoul.jpg

name: Hampi
blurb: Ruined capital of Vijayanagara and its carved stone chariot, 16th century · European visitors compared it to Rome at its height — sacked so thoroughly in 1565 it was never resettled
source: Wikimedia Commons: Stone Chariot at Vittala temple, Hampi.jpg

name: Hereford Mappa Mundi
blurb: Largest surviving medieval world map on a single sheet, c. 1300 · It places Jerusalem dead-centre, east at the top — real kingdoms mixed with Eden and mythical monsters
source: Wikimedia Commons: Hereford-Karte.jpg

name: Jerash
blurb: Roman provincial city in Jordan and its sweeping oval colonnade, 2nd century AD · Its ancient hippodrome still hosts chariot races, re-enacted by actors in Roman legionary costume
source: Wikimedia Commons: Jerash - Oval Forum 02.jpg

name: Great Mosque of Kairouan
blurb: One of Islam's oldest great mosques, in Tunisia, with the world's oldest minaret · Its prayer hall is held up by recycled Roman and Byzantine columns of mismatched heights
source: Wikimedia Commons: Courtyard and minaret of the Great Mosque of Kairouan, Tunisia.jpg

name: Kilwa Kisiwani Ruins
blurb: Coral-stone ruins of a Swahili trading sultanate, Great Mosque built from 11th century · Ibn Battuta called it one of the most beautiful cities he'd seen, built on the gold and ivory trade
source: Wikimedia Commons: Great Mosque Kilwa Kisiwani Tanzania.jpg

name: Kizhi Pogost
blurb: Russia's stacked-dome wooden churches on an island in Lake Onega, built without a single nail, 18th century
source: Wikimedia Commons: Transfiguration Church of Kizhi island.jpg

name: Laocoön and His Sons
blurb: c. 40–30 BC · Vatican Museums, Rome — its 1506 rediscovery in a Roman vineyard was attended by Michelangelo himself, and helped kick off the Renaissance craze for classical sculpture
source: Wikimedia Commons: Laocoon and His Sons.jpg

name: Las Meninas
blurb: Diego Velázquez, 1656 · Museo del Prado, Madrid — Velázquez painted himself into the scene, brush in hand, working on the very canvas we're looking at
source: Wikimedia Commons: Las Meninas, by Diego Velázquez, from Prado in Google Earth.jpg

name: Leptis Magna
blurb: Grand Roman city on the Libyan coast, adorned by the emperor Septimius Severus · Its grandest buildings were funded by Septimius Severus, born right here, Rome's first African-born emperor
source: Wikimedia Commons: Leptis Magna, Al-Khums, Libya 4.jpg

name: Library of Celsus
blurb: Roman marble library facade at Ephesus, c. 117 AD — Celsus himself is buried in a stone sarcophagus beneath it, making his library also his tomb
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ephesus Celsus Library Façade.jpg

name: Longmen Grottoes
blurb: Chinese cliff carved with thousands of Buddhas, crowned by a colossal Vairocana, 7th century · The colossal Buddha's face is thought to resemble Wu Zetian, China's only female emperor
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ancient Buddhist Grottoes at Longmen- Fengxian Temple, Vairocana Buddha.jpg

name: Shore Temple
blurb: Granite temple standing by the Bay of Bengal at Mahabalipuram, 8th century AD · Legend told of six sister temples swallowed by the sea — the 2004 tsunami briefly bared structures offshore
source: Wikimedia Commons: Mamallapuram, Shore Temple, India.jpg

name: Mapungubwe Gold Rhino
blurb: Gold-foil rhinoceros figurine from a royal burial, c. 13th century AD · Under apartheid, authorities downplayed research on the wealthy African kingdom that made it
attribution: Sian Tiley-Nel / University of Pretoria Museums
source: Wikimedia Commons: UP rhino.JPG

name: Matsumoto Castle
blurb: Japan's black-walled 'Crow Castle', a 16th-century keep in the Alps · Unlike most reconstructed Japanese castles, its wooden keep is largely original, its walls black
source: Wikimedia Commons: 松本城 - Matsumoto Castle - Flickr - tsuruta yosuke.jpg

name: Meroë Pyramids
blurb: Steep royal pyramids of the Kushite kings in Sudan, c. 300 BC–300 AD — there are more pyramids here than in all of Egypt
source: Wikimedia Commons: Meroe Pyramids - 33110830438.jpg

name: Mesa Verde
blurb: Ancestral Puebloan cliff dwellings beneath a Colorado canyon rim, 13th century — Cliff Palace is the largest cliff dwelling in North America, abandoned within a generation for reasons still debated
source: Wikimedia Commons: MesaVerdeNationalParkCliffPalace.jpg

name: Nabta Playa Circle
blurb: Prehistoric megalithic calendar circle, c. 4800 BC · Built by cattle-herders in a then-green Sahara, its stones may align to the summer solstice
source: Wikimedia Commons: Calendar aswan.JPG

name: Newgrange
blurb: Ireland's Neolithic passage tomb, carved with spirals and older than Stonehenge and the Great Pyramid of Giza alike, c. 3200 BC
source: Wikimedia Commons: Entrance Stone - Newgrange - Detail.jpg

name: Ollantaytambo
blurb: Inca fortress-town of steep stone terraces in Peru's Sacred Valley, 15th century · The Inca once defeated the Spanish here in battle — nearby, huge 'tired stones' lie where builders left them
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ollantaytambo Inca terraces1.jpg

name: Olympia Stadium
blurb: Stadium of the ancient Games (first held 776 BC); the vaulted entrance is 3rd century BC · Athletes at the ancient Games competed naked — married women were banned from watching, on pain of death
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ancient Olympic Stadium Entrance (5987161338).jpg

name: Palenque
blurb: Maya pyramid-tomb rising from the Chiapas jungle — its ruler Pakal's carved sarcophagus lid is the image conspiracy theorists insist shows an ancient astronaut, 7th century AD
source: Wikimedia Commons: Palenque Temple of Inscriptions.JPG

name: Palmyra
blurb: Roman-era caravan city of Syria — its great arch stood 1,800 years until ISIS dynamited it in 2015
source: Wikimedia Commons: Palmyra - Monumental Arch.jpg

name: Prambanan
blurb: Java's soaring Hindu temple compound of pointed spires, 9th century AD — local legend says it was built in a single night, one temple short of a cursed princess's demand for a thousand
source: Wikimedia Commons: Shiva Temple of Prambanan in Java Indonesia.jpg

name: Sanchi Stupa
blurb: India's great Buddhist stupa and its carved gateways, begun under Ashoka · Its carved gateways never show the Buddha in human form — early art used symbols instead, like a wheel
source: Wikimedia Commons: Stupa 1, Sanchi 02.jpg

name: Shwedagon Pagoda
blurb: Myanmar's great stupa crowning Yangon, plated in tonnes of gold and said to enshrine strands of the Buddha's own hair · Its spire is crowned by a golden orb studded with diamonds, including a 76-carat stone at the very tip
source: Wikimedia Commons: Shwedagon Pagoda, Golden stupa, Yangon, Myanmar.jpg

name: Standard of Ur
blurb: Despite the name, nobody actually knows what it was for — Woolley's 'battle standard' theory has since given way to guesses that it's a lyre soundbox or a treasure chest
source: Wikimedia Commons: Standard of Ur front view.jpg

name: Stone Town Zanzibar Door
blurb: Brass-studded carved wooden door of Swahili-Omani style, 19th century · The brass studs were an Indian design to stop war elephants battering doors — purely decorative by Zanzibar
source: Wikimedia Commons: Detail of Carved Wooden Door - Stone Town - Zanzibar - Tanzania (8841700340).jpg
image_author: Adam Jones from Kelowna, BC, Canada

name: Summer Palace
blurb: Beijing's imperial lakeside garden-palace, rebuilt in the 1880s by the Dowager Empress Cixi — reportedly using funds meant for China's navy
source: Wikimedia Commons: Summer Palace over Kunming Lake and Nanhu Island.jpg
mcq: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte

name: Tara Brooch
blurb: Elaborate Celtic gilt-silver pseudo-penannular brooch, early 8th century AD · Despite the name, it has no link to the Hill of Tara — found near a beach, renamed for marketing
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ireland 2010 etc 029.jpg

name: Tassili Rock Art
blurb: Prehistoric painted rock shelters, c. 10,000-1,000 BC · Its paintings show a Sahara now unrecognisable — giraffes, hippos and crocodiles thriving centuries ago
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Tanzoumaitak cave painting in Tassili n'ajjer.jpg

name: Pyramid of the Sun
blurb: Colossal stepped pyramid at Teotihuacán, Mexico — the third-largest pyramid on Earth, built c. 200 AD by a civilisation whose own name for itself has been lost to time
source: Wikimedia Commons: Pyramid of the Sun, Teotihuacan, from path to parking lot.jpg

name: Tiwanaku
blurb: Andean ceremonial centre and its carved Gate of the Sun, Bolivia, c. 500 AD · By the time the Inca found these ruins, long abandoned, legend credited a race of giants
source: Wikimedia Commons: Bol-tihuanaco-sonnentor.jpg

name: Trajan's Column
blurb: 113 AD · Trajan's Forum, Rome — Trajan's entire Dacian military campaign spirals up the column in relief; unrolled, the frieze would stretch some 200 metres
source: Wikimedia Commons: Trajan's Column (48423812647).jpg

name: Trundholm Sun Chariot
blurb: Bronze Age horse-drawn gilded sun disc on wheels, c. 1400 BC · One face of the sun disc is gilded gold, the other plain bronze — day and night journeys
source: Wikimedia Commons: Solvognen DO-6865 2000.jpg

name: Uxmal
blurb: Pyramid of the Magician, built in five phases, 6th–10th century AD · Legend says it was built overnight by a magical dwarf hatched from an egg, to explain an unusual pyramid
source: Wikimedia Commons: Pyramid of the Magician (Pirámide del Adivino), Zona Arqueológica de Uxmal, Yucatan, Mexico.jpg

name: Warren Cup
blurb: Its explicit homoerotic relief scenes made it too controversial for the British Museum to put on public display for decades after acquiring it
source: Wikimedia Commons: Warren Cup 1.jpg

name: Wawel Castle
blurb: Royal castle on Wawel Hill, mainly 14th-16th century · Legend says a dragon lived in the cave below, tricked by a cobbler into eating a sulphur-stuffed sheep
source: Wikimedia Commons: Royal Castle, Wawel Hill, 4 Wawel, Old Town, Kraków, Poland.jpg

name: Djenne Terracotta
blurb: Hunched terracotta figure from the inland Niger Delta, 13th–15th century · Almost all were looted before excavation, so scholars can't agree who they depict or why they're hunched
source: Wikimedia Commons: Seated figure grom Mali, 13th century, Djenné peoples, Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1981.218.JPG

name: Gedi Ruins
blurb: Ruined Swahili palace town swallowed by forest, 13th–17th century · Chinese porcelain and Persian glass found here show this Kenyan town's Indian Ocean trade links
source: Wikimedia Commons: Palace at Gedi Ruins.jpg

name: Hope Diamond
blurb: Once part of the French Crown Jewels, stolen during the Revolution — it's trailed a 'curse' legend ever since, with owners said to have met ruin, madness, or the guillotine
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Hope Diamond - SIA.jpg

name: Ishango Bone
blurb: Notched bone tally tool, c. 20,000 years old · Some read its notches as an early lunar calendar; others see arithmetic, even prime numbers
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ishango bone.jpg

name: Kerma Deffufa
blurb: Massive mudbrick temple mound, c. 2500-1500 BC · One of the largest ancient structures in sub-Saharan Africa, built by Kerma, which rivalled Egypt
source: Wikimedia Commons: Kerma-Deffufa.jpg

name: Khami Ruins
blurb: Dry-stone royal capital with decorative walling, 15th-17th century · Built as a successor capital after Great Zimbabwe's fall, its walls carry rare checkerboard patterns
source: Wikimedia Commons: Khami Ruins, so-called Monolith Platform.jpg

name: Ziggurat of Ur
blurb: Sumer's stepped brick temple-mountain at Ur, c. 2100 BC — built for the moon god Nanna in the city the Bible names as Abraham's birthplace
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ancient ziggurat at Ali Air Base Iraq 2005.jpg

name: Utrecht Psalter
blurb: Carolingian psalter with vivid pen-sketch illustrations, c. AD 820–835 · Its energetic pen sketches were so influential English scribes copied them centuries later
source: Wikimedia Commons: Utrecht Psalter.jpg
mcq: Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry

name: Winchester Bible
blurb: Largest surviving 12th-century English illuminated bible, c. 1160–1175 · It was never finished — several pages are bare pencil outlines, abandoned mid-illustration
source: Wikimedia Commons: God addressing Jeremiah, Winchester Bible, 1160-75 (22797800517).jpg

name: Terentius Neo and His Wife
variants: portrait of the baker and his wife
blurb: Fresco portrait of a Pompeii baker and his wife, 1st century AD, buried by Vesuvius in 79 · Both husband and wife hold writing tools, signalling a rare Roman portrait of shared literacy
source: Wikimedia Commons: MANNapoli 9058 couple painting.jpg

name: Titanic
blurb: White Star liner, sank in the North Atlantic on 15 April 1912 · Her radio operators sent both the old CQD distress call and the brand-new SOS, making her one of the first ships to use it at sea
source: Wikimedia Commons: RMS Titanic 3.jpg

name: United States Declaration of Independence
blurb: Adopted by the Second Continental Congress, 4 July 1776 · Most of the signatures we see today weren't added until 2 August — only Hancock and the secretary signed on the day itself
attribution: original: Second Continental Congress; reproduction: William Stone
source: Wikimedia Commons: United States Declaration of Independence.jpg
image_author: original: Second Continental Congress; reproduction: William Stone

name: United States Constitution
blurb: Signed at the Philadelphia Convention, 17 September 1787 · At roughly 4,400 words, it's the shortest written constitution of any major world power still in force
source: Wikimedia Commons: Constitution of the United States - DPLA - 9ca804144bd5965e992ae3528bc3c6a3 (page 1).jpg

name: Berlin Wall
blurb: Divided East and West Berlin from 13 August 1961 to 9 November 1989 · West Berliners covered their side in graffiti for decades — the East German side stayed a blank, heavily guarded 'death strip'
source: Wikimedia Commons: Berlinermauer.jpg

name: Empire State Building
blurb: Completed in 1931 in just 410 days · Its planned mooring mast for airships was abandoned after one attempt nearly blew a delivery blimp off its tether
source: Wikimedia Commons: NARA Empire State Building.jpg
image_author: War Department, Army Air Forces; photographer not named

name: Space Shuttle
blurb: NASA's reusable orbiter fleet, first flew in 1981 · Discovery alone flew 39 missions — more spaceflights than any other single spacecraft in history
source: Wikimedia Commons: STS120LaunchHiRes-edit1.jpg

name: World Trade Center
blurb: Twin towers completed 1972–1973 · The north tower briefly held the world's-tallest-building title before Chicago's Sears Tower overtook it in 1973
source: Wikimedia Commons: World Trade Center, New York City - aerial view (March 2001).jpg

name: White House
blurb: Home to every US president since 1800 · British troops burned it in August 1814 — a sudden thunderstorm that same night likely saved its stone walls from total collapse
source: Wikimedia Commons: WhiteHouseSouthFacade.JPG

name: Kaaba
blurb: Cube-shaped shrine at the centre of Mecca's Grand Mosque, rebuilt in its current form in 1629–1630 · The black silk kiswah draping it is taken down and rewoven fresh every single year for Hajj
source: Wikimedia Commons: Kaaba2.JPG

name: Louvre
blurb: Former royal palace turned museum, opened to the public in 1793 · Its glass pyramid entrance, added in 1989, was so controversial at first that critics compared it to a dagger through the historic courtyard
source: Wikimedia Commons: Cour Napoléon at night - Louvre.jpg

name: Shroud of Turin
blurb: Linen cloth bearing a faint body image, first documented in the 1350s · Radiocarbon dating in 1988 placed its fabric in the medieval period, though disputes over the test continue
source: Wikimedia Commons: Shroudofturin1.jpg

name: Saturn V
blurb: NASA's Moon rocket, first launched in 1967 · Across all 13 flights — Apollo 4 through 17 plus the Skylab launch — it never suffered a single failure
source: Wikimedia Commons: Apollo 11 Launch2.jpg

name: Domesday Book
blurb: William the Conqueror's survey of England, completed in 1086 · Its findings were so exhaustive and final that Anglo-Saxons nicknamed it 'Domesday' after the Last Judgement — nothing in it could be appealed
source: Wikimedia Commons: Domesday zinco Somerset Glastonbury.jpg

name: Little Boy
blurb: Uranium gun-type bomb dropped on Hiroshima, 6 August 1945 · Unlike its plutonium cousin tested at Trinity that July, Little Boy's design was never test-fired before that first live drop
attribution: US Atomic Energy Commission (now US Department of Energy)
source: Wikimedia Commons: Little Boy bomb.jpg
image_author: US Atomic Energy Commission (now US Department of Energy)

name: HMS Victory
blurb: Nelson's flagship at Trafalgar, launched in 1765 · She's still a commissioned Royal Navy warship today, the oldest in the world still on the active list
source: Wikimedia Commons: Victory Portsmouth um 1900.jpg

name: Ajanta Caves
blurb: Buddhist rock-cut cave complex, carved between the 2nd century BC and 6th century AD · Abandoned for over a thousand years, it was only rediscovered in 1819 when a British officer chasing a tiger stumbled on one entrance
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ajanta cave no. 9 2010.jpg

name: Sydney Opera House
blurb: Jørn Utzon's harbour-side design, opened in 1973 · The sail-like shells took over a decade longer to engineer than planned, since no one had worked out how to actually build the curved roof shapes he'd sketched
source: Wikimedia Commons: 00 1375 Sydney Opera House (Australia).jpg

name: Voyager Golden Record
blurb: Gold-plated phonograph disc launched aboard both Voyager probes in 1977 · It carries a sample of uranium-238 etched into its cover, so any finder could calculate exactly how long it had been travelling
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Sounds of Earth Record Cover - GPN-2000-001978.jpg

name: Palace of Westminster
blurb: Seat of the UK Parliament, rebuilt after an 1834 fire destroyed almost the whole medieval palace · Only Westminster Hall, with its 14th-century hammerbeam roof, survived largely intact
source: Wikimedia Commons: Houses of Parliament in 2022 (cropped).jpg
image_author: Terry Ott from Washington, DC Metro Area, United States of America

name: Sistine Chapel
blurb: Pope Sixtus IV's private chapel, completed in 1483 · Its side walls were frescoed by an earlier generation of masters — Botticelli and Perugino among them — years before Michelangelo ever touched the ceiling
source: Wikimedia Commons: Sistina-interno.jpg

name: USS Constitution
blurb: Commissioned in 1797 · Nicknamed 'Old Ironsides' after War of 1812 sailors swore they saw British cannonballs bounce off her oak hull — she's still a commissioned US Navy ship today, the oldest afloat in the world
attribution: U.S. Navy photo by Seaman Matthew R. Fairchild/Released (140704-N-OG138-866)
source: Wikimedia Commons: USS Constitution fires a 17-gun salute.jpg
image_author: U.S. Navy photo by Seaman Matthew R. Fairchild/Released (140704-N-OG138-866)

name: United States Capitol
blurb: Its cast-iron dome was finished in 1866, after Lincoln insisted construction continue all through the Civil War as proof the Union would endure — the bronze Statue of Freedom was hoisted onto the very top in December 1863
attribution: Architect of the Capitol; derivative work: O.J.
source: Wikimedia Commons: United States Capitol west front edit2 (cropped).jpg
image_author: Architect of the Capitol; derivative crop by O.J.

name: British Museum
blurb: Britain's first national public museum, opened its doors in 1759 · It has never charged general admission in over 260 years, a condition written into the founding Act of Parliament
source: Wikimedia Commons: British Museum from NE 2 (cropped).JPG

name: Koh-i-Noor
blurb: Seized by the British East India Company in 1849 · A legend claims the diamond curses any man who wears it — every royal owner since has been a queen or queen consort
source: Wikimedia Commons: Replica of the Koh-i-Noor (cropped).jpg

name: Temple of Artemis
blurb: One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, rebuilt after a fire in 356 BC · Legend says it burned down the same night Alexander the Great was born, allegedly torched by a man seeking eternal fame
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ephesos.jpg

name: Enola Gay
blurb: Dropped the atomic bomb 'Little Boy' on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 · Pilot Paul Tibbets named the B-29 after his own mother the night before the mission
source: Wikimedia Commons: Enola Gay (plane).jpg

name: Lighthouse of Alexandria
blurb: Built c. 280 BC on the island of Pharos · It stood for over 1,600 years until earthquakes toppled it for good in the 14th century — no photograph or accurate scale drawing survives, only ancient descriptions and coins
source: Wikimedia Commons: Lighthouse - Thiersch.png

name: Church of the Holy Sepulchre
blurb: This Crusader-era church was consecrated in 1149 on the site venerated as Christ's crucifixion and burial place · A wooden ladder left on a windowsill has stayed there since at least 1728, because moving it would break the fragile 'status quo' agreement between its rival Christian custodians
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre-Jerusalem.JPG

name: Red Fort
blurb: Shah Jahan's citadel for his new capital was completed in 1648 · Every Indian Prime Minister has delivered the nation's Independence Day speech from its ramparts since 1947
source: Wikimedia Commons: Red Fort, Delhi by alexfurr.jpg

name: St Paul's Cathedral
blurb: Christopher Wren's masterpiece was completed in 1710, after the Great Fire destroyed its medieval predecessor · A 1940 photograph of its dome rising through Blitz smoke, captioned 'St Paul's Survives', became one of the most famous images of the Second World War
source: Wikimedia Commons: St Pauls aerial (cropped).jpg

name: Chrysler Building
blurb: Completed in 1930 · Its stainless-steel spire was secretly built in pieces inside the fire shaft and hoisted into place in about 90 minutes, a surprise move that let it beat a rival tower to become the world's tallest building — for less than a year
source: Wikimedia Commons: Chrysler Building 2007.JPG

name: Colossus of Rhodes
blurb: Erected around 280 BC to celebrate Rhodes surviving a year-long siege · It toppled in an earthquake after just 54 years standing — contrary to popular legend, it never straddled the harbour entrance with ships passing beneath its legs
source: Wikimedia Commons: Colossus Rhodius ex Athanasius Kircher - Turris Babel - 1679 (page 133 crop).jpg

name: Metropolitan Museum of Art
blurb: Founded in 1870 by a group of American businessmen, financiers and artists who wanted a national art institution to rival Europe's · Its collection now spans over 5,000 years of world culture and some 2 million objects
source: Wikimedia Commons: Metropolitan Museum of Art (The Met) - Central Park, NYC.jpg

name: Hoover Dam
blurb: Completed in 1936, two years ahead of schedule · Engineers embedded cooling pipes in the concrete because a mass that size would otherwise still be curing today — it would have taken over a century to cool naturally on its own
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ansel Adams - National Archives 79-AAB-01.jpg

name: Voynich Manuscript
blurb: Carbon-dated to 1404-1438 · Its unknown script has defeated every attempt at decryption for over a century, including a 1940s US Army study group led by cryptographer William Friedman, famed for breaking Japanese wartime codes
source: Wikimedia Commons: Voynich Manuscript (32).jpg

name: Washington Monument
blurb: Construction stalled for over two decades and resumed only in 1877 · By then the marble supply had changed, leaving a visible colour change roughly a third of the way up the obelisk that's still there today
source: Wikimedia Commons: Washington 250424 Washington Monument 01.jpg

name: Al-Aqsa Mosque
blurb: Islam's third-holiest site, first built in the early 8th century AD and rebuilt repeatedly after earthquakes · Its silver dome only reached its current look in 1983, replacing an anodized aluminium roof installed after a 1969 arson attack
source: Wikimedia Commons: Jerusalem-2013-Temple Mount-Al-Aqsa Mosque (NE exposure).jpg

name: Hanging Gardens of Babylon
blurb: Said to have been built by King Nebuchadnezzar II around 600 BC for a homesick wife who missed the mountains of her homeland · No archaeological trace of the gardens has ever been found in Babylon itself, leading some historians to argue they actually stood in Nineveh, over 300 miles away
source: Wikimedia Commons: Babylon; the city (above); the hanging gardens of Babylon Wellcome L0047679.jpg

name: Vasa
blurb: Swedish warship that capsized less than a mile into her maiden voyage in 1628 · Raised almost fully intact 333 years later, in 1961
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Vasa from the Bow.jpg

name: Musée d'Orsay
blurb: A former Beaux-Arts railway station built for the 1900 Paris World's Fair, converted into a museum of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist art in 1986
source: Wikimedia Commons: MuseeDOrsay.jpg

name: Guernica
blurb: Picasso's response to the German bombing of the Basque town of Guernica on 26 April 1937, painted in weeks for the Paris World's Fair
source: Wikimedia Commons: Mural del "Guernica" de Picasso.jpg

name: Buddhas of Bamiyan
blurb: Two 6th-century sandstone Buddhas up to 55 metres tall, carved into a cliff face in Afghanistan · Dynamited by the Taliban in March 2001
source: Wikimedia Commons: Buddha of Bamiyan.jpg

name: Topkapi Palace
blurb: Ottoman sultans ruled from this sprawling Istanbul palace complex from the 1460s until the 19th century, when they moved to the newer Dolmabahçe
source: Wikimedia Commons: Topkapi Palace Seen From Harem.JPG

name: Kannon
blurb: Originally the male bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, reimagined as a compassionate female deity in China by around the 10th century AD · Venerated ever since as Guanyin in China and Kannon in Japan
source: Wikimedia Commons: Statue of Guanyin, February 5, 2019 (3) (cropped).jpg

name: Mausoleum at Halicarnassus
blurb: Built around 350 BC as the tomb of the Persian satrap Mausolus — one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and the origin of the word "mausoleum"
source: Wikimedia Commons: The ruins of the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus.jpg

name: Çatalhöyük
blurb: One of the world's earliest large farming settlements, inhabited c. 7100–5700 BC · Houses were entered through holes in the roof, with no streets or doors at ground level
source: Wikimedia Commons: CatalHoyukSouthArea.JPG

name: Valley of the Kings
blurb: Burial ground for New Kingdom pharaohs from the 16th to the 11th century BC · Over 60 tombs have been found here, including Tutankhamun's in 1922
source: Wikimedia Commons: Luxor, Tal der Könige (1995, 860x605).jpg

name: St Edward's Crown
blurb: Solid-gold coronation crown remade in 1661 for Charles II after Parliament melted down the medieval original · Used to crown every British monarch since
source: Wikimedia Commons: Saint Edward's Crown.jpg

name: Cullinan Diamond
blurb: Found in a South African mine in 1905 at 3,106 carats — still the largest gem-quality rough diamond ever discovered · Later cut into stones set in the Sovereign's Sceptre and Crown Jewels
source: Wikimedia Commons: Cullinan diamond rough.jpg

name: Cutty Sark
blurb: Built in 1869 as one of the last and fastest tea clippers · Now preserved in dry dock at Greenwich, raised on glass to reveal her copper-clad hull
source: Wikimedia Commons: Cutty Sark (16719233476).jpg

name: Maitreya
blurb: Carved from a single piece of red-pine in 7th-century Japan · One of the first objects Japan ever designated a National Treasure, in 1951
source: Wikimedia Commons: Maitreya Koryuji.JPG

name: Reichstag building
blurb: Built in 1894 to house the German parliament · Gutted by fire in 1933 and by WWII bombing, it reopened in 1999 under Norman Foster's glass dome
source: Wikimedia Commons: Reichstagsgebäude von Westen.jpg

name: Sydney Harbour Bridge
blurb: Opened in 1932 and nicknamed "the Coathanger" for its arch · A horseman famously slashed the ribbon before the official opening, forcing a second cut
source: Wikimedia Commons: SydneyHarbourBridge1 gobeirne.jpg

name: Victoria and Albert Museum
blurb: Founded in 1852 after the Great Exhibition, its collection spans 5,000 years of art and design — including a full-size plaster cast of Trajan's Column, split in two to fit
source: Wikimedia Commons: Victoria & Albert Museum Entrance, London, UK - Diliff.jpg

name: Cahokia
blurb: Largest earthwork in the pre-Columbian Americas north of Mexico · Built and occupied c. 1050–1350 AD, its main mound covers more ground than the Great Pyramid of Giza
source: Wikimedia Commons: Monks Mound in July.JPG

name: Pergamon
blurb: Hilltop Anatolian acropolis whose 2nd-century AD Temple of Trajan still stands among its ruins · The ancient city's library reportedly held 200,000 scrolls, rivalling Alexandria's
source: Wikimedia Commons: Temple of Trajan, Pergamon 01.jpg

name: Queen Elizabeth 2
blurb: Cunard ocean liner launched in 1967, serving as fleet flagship for nearly four decades · Retired to Dubai in 2008 to become a floating hotel
source: Wikimedia Commons: RMS Queen Elizabeth 2 in Trondheim 2008.jpg

name: Susa
blurb: Capital of ancient Elam and a favourite residence of Persian kings from Darius I onward · Sacked by the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal in 647 BC and later revived under the Achaemenids
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Apadana, a large hypostyle room of 36 columns in the Palace of Darius, Susa, capital of Elam and of the Achaemenid Empire, Iran (46950284624).jpg

name: Amber Room
blurb: Gifted to Peter the Great by Prussia in 1716, looted by Nazi forces in 1941 and never found again · This hall reopened in 2003 as an exact reconstruction at Catherine Palace
source: Wikimedia Commons: Catherine Palace interior - Amber Room (1).jpg
mcq: Malachite Room of the Winter Palace

name: Canterbury Cathedral
variants: the cathedral church of christ, canterbury
blurb: Mother church of the Church of England, largely rebuilt after a fire in 1174 · Archbishop Thomas Becket was hacked down by four knights in the north transept in 1170, turning the cathedral into medieval Europe's pilgrimage blockbuster
source: Wikimedia Commons: Canterbury Cathedral - Portal Nave Cross-spire.jpeg

name: Masada
blurb: Herod's desert fortress-palace above the Dead Sea, expanded around 30 BC · Besieging Romans built a stone ramp still visible today, and in 73 AD found the defenders had chosen mass suicide over capture
source: Wikimedia Commons: Israel-2013-Aerial 21-Masada.jpg

name: Mary Rose
blurb: Henry VIII's flagship, launched in 1511 · Sank right in front of him in the Solent in 1545, then spent 437 years on the seabed before divers raised her hull in 1982
source: Wikimedia Commons: Mary Rose in Mary Rose Museum 2023-05-05.jpg

name: Prado Museum
blurb: Madrid's Royal Museum of Paintings, opened to the public in 1819 · The Neoclassical building was actually designed in 1785 as a natural science academy, before Spain's royal art collection took it over
source: Wikimedia Commons: Museo del Prado 2016 (25185969599).jpg

name: The Garden of Earthly Delights
blurb: Hieronymus Bosch's surreal triptych, painted around 1500 · A musical score inked onto a damned soul's backside in the Hell panel was transcribed and performed centuries later, going viral as 'the 500-year-old butt song from hell'
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Garden of Earthly Delights by Bosch High Resolution 2.jpg
mcq: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog

name: Tokyo Tower
blurb: Tokyo's steel broadcast tower, completed in 1958 · Part of its frame was forged from scrapped American tanks damaged in the Korean War, and it stands taller than the Eiffel Tower it deliberately outdid
source: Wikimedia Commons: Tokyo Tower 2023.jpg

name: Taxila
blurb: Ancient Gandharan city that Alexander the Great's army marched through in 326 BC · Under the Kushans it became a Buddhist university town, its scholars said to have taught medicine, astronomy, and the fine art of memorising sacred texts by heart
source: Wikimedia Commons: Double-Headed Eagle Stupa at Sirkap 08.jpg

name: Statue of Zeus at Olympia
blurb: Phidias's ivory-and-gold statue of Zeus, completed around 435 BC · One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, it reportedly stood over 12 metres tall and was probably lost to a fire in Constantinople around 475 AD
source: Wikimedia Commons: Le Jupiter Olympien ou l'art de la sculpture antique 1.jpg

name: Uffizi
blurb: Vasari's 1560s office block for the Medici administration ('uffizi' literally means offices) · A secret elevated corridor he built in just five months in 1565 still lets you walk from here to the Pitti Palace without touching a public street
source: Wikimedia Commons: Florence, Italy - panoramio (125).jpg
mcq: Monastery and Site of the Escorial

name: American Museum of Natural History
blurb: New York's American Museum of Natural History, founded in 1869 · The 34-tonne Cape York meteorite in its meteorite hall is so heavy its support column runs straight down through the building to bedrock
source: Wikimedia Commons: American Museum of Natural History 02.jpg

name: Appian Way
blurb: Rome's 'queen of roads,' begun in 312 BC by censor Appius Claudius · After crushing Spartacus's slave revolt in 71 BC, Crassus lined this road with the crucified bodies of 6,000 rebels for the final miles into Rome
source: Wikimedia Commons: Appian Way.jpg

name: L'Anse aux Meadows National Historic Site
variants: l'anse aux meadows national historic site
blurb: Newfoundland's Norse settlement, precisely tree-ring dated to 1021 AD by a cosmic-ray spike in the wood · It's the only confirmed Viking site in North America, put there almost five centuries before Columbus
attribution: Dylan Kereluk from White Rock, Canada
source: Wikimedia Commons: Authentic Viking recreation.jpg

name: Natural History Museum, London
blurb: London's Natural History Museum, opened in 1881 · Its terracotta facade is crawling with sculpted animals — extinct species carved on the west wing, living species on the east, the building itself picking a side
source: Wikimedia Commons: Entrance to Natural History Museum, Cromwell Road, London SW7 - geograph.org.uk - 1034304.jpg

name: Lincoln Memorial
blurb: Washington's marble temple to Lincoln, dedicated in 1922 · Its 36 columns stand for the 36 states in the Union when he died, and its steps hosted Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' speech in 1963
source: Wikimedia Commons: Aerial view of Lincoln Memorial - east side EDIT.jpeg

name: Monastery and Site of the Escorial
variants: monastery and site of the escorial
royal seat of san lorenzo de el escorial
blurb: Philip II's granite palace-monastery, built 1563–1584 to fulfil a vow after his victory at Saint-Quentin · Its grid-shaped floor plan honours St Lawrence, martyred on a gridiron, and the king ruled his empire from a small room where he could watch Mass from his deathbed
source: Wikimedia Commons: Monasterio de El Escorial en Madrid.jpg

name: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog
variants: wanderer above the sea of fog
the wanderer above the sea of fog
wanderer above a sea of fog
blurb: Caspar David Friedrich's Romantic icon, painted around 1818 · The craggy peaks are a total invention — Friedrich collaged them from several real outcrops in the Elbe Sandstone Mountains, no such view actually exists
source: Wikimedia Commons: Friedrich, Caspar David - Wanderer über dem Nebelmeer.jpg

name: Centre Pompidou
blurb: Paris's inside-out museum, opened in 1977 · Its pipework is colour-coded by function — blue for air conditioning, green for water, yellow for electricity, red for the escalators and lifts
source: Wikimedia Commons: Centre Pompidou, seen from Tour Montparnasse.jpg

name: Saint Catherine's Monastery
variants: monastery of the god-trodden mount sinai
blurb: A Byzantine emperor had this fortress-monastery built between 548 and 565 AD at the foot of Mount Sinai, on the spot tradition marks as the Burning Bush · It's the oldest continuously inhabited Christian monastery on Earth
source: Wikimedia Commons: Katharinenkloster Sinai BW 2.jpg

name: Peacock Throne
blurb: Shah Jahan's jewel-encrusted golden throne, finished in 1635 after seven years' work · Contemporaries reckoned its gems cost twice as much as the Taj Mahal, and Persian invader Nader Shah hauled it off to Iran in 1739
source: Wikimedia Commons: Shah Jahan op de pauwentroon.jpg

name: Umayyad Mosque
blurb: Caliph al-Walid I built this Damascus mosque between 706 and 715 AD, atop a Roman temple and a Christian basilica · A shrine inside still claims to hold the head of John the Baptist, honoured by Muslim and Christian visitors alike
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ommayyad masjed.jpg

name: Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka
blurb: Indian rock shelters holding some of the subcontinent's oldest art, the earliest paintings estimated at roughly 10,000 years old · Archaeologist V.S. Wakankar rediscovered the site in 1957 after the hills reminded him of France's painted caves
source: Wikimedia Commons: Bhimbetka Cave Paintings.jpg

name: Khufu ship
blurb: Buried beside the Great Pyramid around 2500 BC and rediscovered in 1954 · The 1,224 disassembled cedar pieces were painstakingly rebuilt over a decade without a single nail — the planks are lashed together with rope
attribution: No machine-readable author provided. Bradipus assumed (based on copyright claims).
source: Wikimedia Commons: Barque Solaire4.JPG

name: Rijksmuseum
blurb: Dutch national museum in Amsterdam, opened 1885 · Designed with a public passage straight through the building for cyclists, who fought (and won) to keep it during a 2013 renovation
source: Wikimedia Commons: Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.jpg

name: Ancient Merv
variants: state historical and cultural park ancient merv
blurb: Silk Road oasis city in Turkmenistan, sacked by the Mongols in 1221 · Was briefly one of the largest cities on Earth just before its destruction
source: Wikimedia Commons: Merv City Walls (10) (44747325714).jpg

name: Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus
blurb: Mumbai's Victorian Gothic railway terminus, opened 1887 · Originally named Victoria Terminus, renamed for the Maratha king Shivaji in 1996
source: Wikimedia Commons: Chatrapati Shivaji Terminus Pano.jpg

name: Tate Modern
blurb: London art museum opened 2000 inside a former power station · Its architect, Giles Gilbert Scott, also designed the classic red telephone box
source: Wikimedia Commons: Tate Modern viewed from Thames Pleasure Boat - geograph.org.uk - 307445.jpg

name: Flatiron Building
blurb: Wedge-shaped Manhattan skyscraper completed 1902 · Its triangular shape comes from squeezing onto a leftover sliver where Broadway crosses Fifth Avenue
source: Wikimedia Commons: Edificio Fuller (Flatiron) en 2010 desde el Empire State crop boxin.jpg

name: National Gallery of Art
variants: national gallery of art west building
blurb: Washington DC's West Building opened 1941 · Funded entirely by banker Andrew Mellon, who insisted the museum never be named after him
source: Wikimedia Commons: National Gallery of Art - West Building.JPG

name: Mahabodhi Temple
blurb: Buddhist temple in Bodh Gaya marking the spot of the Buddha's enlightenment, current tower rebuilt c. 5th–6th century CE · Restored again in the 1880s by British archaeologist Alexander Cunningham
source: Wikimedia Commons: Mahabodhitemple.jpg

name: Mikasa
blurb: Japanese flagship at the Battle of Tsushima, 1905 · Now preserved in Yokosuka as the world's last surviving pre-dreadnought battleship
source: Wikimedia Commons: Yokosuka-mikasa-08-2010.png

name: Cyrene
blurb: Ancient Greek colony in Libya founded c. 631 BC by settlers from the island of Thera · These Roman baths were rebuilt after Jewish rebels sacked the city in 115 AD
source: Wikimedia Commons: CireneTermeTraiano.jpg

name: Vatican Museums
blurb: Papal art collection founded by Pope Julius II in 1506 · Today over 6 million visitors a year file out through a spiralling double-helix staircase
source: Wikimedia Commons: Mura vaticane - ingresso ai Musei 00410.JPG
mcq: Monastery and Site of the Escorial

name: Seville Cathedral
variants: cathedral of saint mary of the see
blurb: World's largest Gothic cathedral by volume, completed 1506 on the site of a mosque · Its bell tower, La Giralda, is the mosque's former minaret, barely altered
source: Wikimedia Commons: DOsaYphXUAIjSGu.jpg large.jpg

name: Hollywood Sign
blurb: Los Angeles hillside sign erected 1923 as a real-estate advert reading 'Hollywoodland' · The last four letters were dropped in 1949
source: Wikimedia Commons: Hollywood Sign (Zuschnitt).jpg

name: Gateway Arch
blurb: St. Louis monument completed 1965 to a design by Eero Saarinen · At 630 feet it's the tallest arch on Earth, and its curve is a mathematically perfect catenary
source: Wikimedia Commons: St Louis Gateway Arch.jpg

name: Elephanta Caves
blurb: Rock-cut Hindu cave temples on an island near Mumbai, carved c. 5th–8th century AD · Named by Portuguese sailors after a giant stone elephant statue that once stood at the dock
source: Wikimedia Commons: Elephanta Caves, India.jpg

name: Port Royal
blurb: Jamaican pirate port once called 'the wickedest city on Earth' · A 1692 earthquake and tsunami swallowed two-thirds of it into the sea within minutes
source: Wikimedia Commons: Aerial view of Port Royal Jamaica.JPG

name: Badshahi Mosque
blurb: Lahore mosque built in 1673 under Mughal emperor Aurangzeb · It stayed the largest mosque in the world for close to 300 years
source: Wikimedia Commons: Badshahi Mosque July 1 2005 pic32 by Ali Imran (1).jpg

name: Hattusa
blurb: Bronze-Age capital of the Hittite Empire, flourishing c. 1650–1200 BC · Its clay-tablet archive preserved the world's oldest known peace treaty, signed with Egypt's Ramesses II
source: Wikimedia Commons: Lion Gate, Hattusa 13 (cropped).jpg

name: Rule of Saint Benedict
blurb: Guidebook for monastic life written by Benedict of Nursia c. 530 AD · This Oxford manuscript, copied within roughly two centuries of his death, is the rule's oldest surviving copy
source: Wikimedia Commons: MS. Hatton 48 fol. 6v-7r.jpg
mcq: Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry

name: Fram
blurb: Norwegian polar exploration ship launched 1892 · Carried Roald Amundsen to the South Pole in 1911, having already carried Fridtjof Nansen to a record northern latitude two decades earlier
source: Wikimedia Commons: Amundsen-Fram.jpg

name: Codex Alexandrinus
blurb: A 5th-century Greek Bible manuscript, one of the oldest nearly-complete copies in existence · Gifted to England's Charles I in 1627 by Constantinople's patriarch
source: Wikimedia Commons: Codex Alexandrinus 013a Mc 6,27-54.JPG

name: Quba Mosque
blurb: First mosque built in Islamic history, founded by Muhammad in 622 AD on his arrival in Medina · Today's structure follows a modern renovation completed in 1986
source: Wikimedia Commons: Quba Mosque from Afar (2024).jpg

name: Spirit of St. Louis
blurb: Custom-built monoplane that carried Charles Lindbergh solo across the Atlantic in 1927 · With no forward window, Lindbergh used a periscope to see straight ahead
source: Wikimedia Commons: Spirit of St Louis Smithsonian 01 2012 258.jpg

name: Sunflowers
variants: still life vase with twelve sunflowers
blurb: Van Gogh, 1888 (Munich version) · In 1912 the Neue Pinakothek became the first public museum in the world to buy one of his paintings
source: Wikimedia Commons: Vincent Willem van Gogh 128.jpg

name: Forth Bridge
blurb: Completed in 1890 as the world's first major steel cantilever bridge · Relentless repainting became so proverbial it entered the language as 'painting the Forth Bridge' — until a 2011 recoat finally came with a 25-year guarantee
source: Wikimedia Commons: Forthbridge feb 2013.jpg

name: Hawa Mahal
blurb: Built in 1799 for the women of Jaipur's royal household · Its five-tier pink facade is pierced by 953 tiny windows yet is only one room deep behind them
source: Wikimedia Commons: East facade Hawa Mahal Jaipur from ground level (July 2022) - img 01.jpg

name: Imperial Regalia of Japan
blurb: Mythologised since Japan's Kojiki chronicle was compiled in 712 AD · Reportedly no reigning emperor has ever seen all three treasures together — they're kept apart, wrapped, and never publicly displayed
source: Wikimedia Commons: 三種の神器 1200x1200.png

name: Van Gogh Museum
blurb: Opened in Amsterdam in 1973 to house the world's largest Van Gogh collection · Its architect, Gerrit Rietveld, died nine years before its doors ever opened
source: Wikimedia Commons: Van Gogh Museum.jpg

name: Independence Hall
blurb: Completed in 1753 as the Pennsylvania State House · Both the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution were signed under this one roof, eleven years apart
source: Wikimedia Commons: Exterior of the Independence Hall, Aug 2019.jpg

name: Art Institute of Chicago
blurb: Opened for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition · The two bronze lions added a year later are nicknamed 'Stand' and 'Roar' and get dressed in jerseys whenever a Chicago team makes the playoffs
source: Wikimedia Commons: Art Institute of Chicago (51575570710).jpg

name: Lahore Fort
blurb: Rebuilt in red sandstone from 1566 under Akbar, with later Mughal additions including the mirrored Sheesh Mahal · One candle's flame there multiplies into a thousand reflected stars
source: Wikimedia Commons: Lahore Fort view from Baradari.jpg

name: Tabula Rogeriana
blurb: Finished in 1154 for King Roger II of Sicily after 15 years' work · A giant silver planisphere of the same map, said to weigh over 100kg, was destroyed by rioters within years of its making
attribution: TabulaRogeriana.jpg : Al-Idrisi (original map), Konrad Miller (current map) *derivative work: PHGCOM ( talk ) (rotation)
source: Wikimedia Commons: TabulaRogeriana upside-down.jpg
image_author: TabulaRogeriana.jpg : Al-Idrisi (original map), Konrad Miller (current map) *derivative work: PHGCOM ( talk ) (rotation)

name: Park Güell
blurb: Designed by Antoni Gaudí from 1900 as a luxury housing estate · Only two of the planned 60 houses were ever built, and Gaudí himself lived in one for nearly 20 years
source: Wikimedia Commons: Güell BCN edited.jpg

name: Egyptian Museum, Cairo
blurb: Opened on Cairo's Tahrir Square in 1902 · Tutankhamun's treasures sat in the same un-air-conditioned display cases there for over a century before finally moving out in the 2020s
source: Wikimedia Commons: 1897 bis 1902 wurde das Ägyptische Museum in Kairo gebaut. 04.jpg

name: The Motherland Calls
blurb: Unveiled in 1967 atop Mamayev Kurgan, the hill where the fiercest fighting of Stalingrad raged · At 85 metres tall it was, for over a decade, the tallest statue on Earth
source: Wikimedia Commons: Волгоград. Мамев курган. Родина-мать зовет.jpg

name: Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry
variants: tres riches heures du duc de berry
book of hours of the duke of berry
blurb: Begun around 1412 by the Limbourg brothers for the Duke of Berry · All three brothers and their patron died within months of each other in 1416, leaving pages like this one unfinished for 70 years
source: Wikimedia Commons: Anatomical Man.jpg

name: National Air and Space Museum
blurb: Opened on the National Mall in 1976, days before the US Bicentennial · It became, within its first year, one of the most-visited museums on Earth
source: Wikimedia Commons: Smithsonian Air and Space Museum.jpg

name: Aachen Cathedral
blurb: Consecrated in 805 AD as Charlemagne's palace chapel · German kings were crowned inside for over five centuries, and in 1978 it became one of the first sites ever named a UNESCO World Heritage Site
source: Wikimedia Commons: Aachen Germany Imperial-Cathedral-01.jpg

name: Daigo Fukuryū Maru
blurb: Caught in radioactive fallout from the US 'Castle Bravo' H-bomb test in 1954 · The crew's ash-dusted return helped inspire that same year's Godzilla and ignited Japan's anti-nuclear movement
source: Wikimedia Commons: Daigo Fukuryū Maru 01.JPG

name: Daria-i-Noor
blurb: Looted from the Mughal treasury during Nader Shah's 1739 sack of Delhi, likely a sister-stone to the Koh-i-Noor · At roughly 182 carats it's one of the largest pink diamonds on Earth
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Daria-e Noor (Sea of Light) Diamond from the collection of the national jewels of Iran at Central Bank of Islamic Republic of Iran.jpg

name: The Kiss (Klimt)
blurb: Painted in 1907-08 during Klimt's 'Golden Phase' · Real gold leaf went into the paint, a nod to his father's trade as a gold engraver, and the Austrian state bought it straight off the exhibition wall
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Kiss - Gustav Klimt - Google Cultural Institute.jpg
mcq: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog

name: Royal Palace of Caserta
blurb: Built from 1752 for the Bourbon kings of Naples to out-do Versailles · Its 1,200 rooms later doubled as the royal palace of Naboo in the Star Wars prequels
source: Wikimedia Commons: Aerial image of the Palace of Caserta (view from the south).jpg

name: Hindenburg
blurb: The largest flying machine ever built caught fire while docking at Lakehurst, New Jersey on 6 May 1937 · Radio reporter Herbert Morrison's anguished live broadcast, 'Oh, the humanity!', made it one of the first disasters ever captured in real time
source: Wikimedia Commons: German airship "Hindenburg" at Lakehurst, New Jersey. - NARA - 518856.tif

name: The Little Mermaid (statue)
blurb: Unveiled in Copenhagen harbour in 1913 · She's been beheaded twice and lost an arm to vandals, yet remains one of the most photographed statues on Earth
source: Wikimedia Commons: Denmark, Copenhagen, Little Mermaid, Langelinie Promenade 150422-25.jpg

name: Villa of the Mysteries
blurb: Frescoed around 60–50 BC · The room's continuous, life-size frieze is one of antiquity's best-preserved paintings, believed to show a bride's initiation into the cult of Dionysus — buried by Vesuvius in AD 79 and not excavated until 1909
source: Wikimedia Commons: Roman fresco Villa dei Misteri Pompeii 009.jpg

name: Priapus of the House of the Vettii
variants: priapus of the house of the vettii
blurb: Painted beside the front door of a rich Pompeian house, before AD 79 · Priapus weighs his manhood against a bag of gold — not a boast but a doorbell for luck: Romans hung outrageous phalluses at thresholds to stare down the evil eye
source: Wikimedia Commons: Pompeya erótica6.jpg
